# Industrial Chemical Processes

## Core ideas and reasoning

Industrial chemistry applies reactions at scale under economic, environmental and safety constraints. A high equilibrium yield alone is not enough if the rate is impractically slow. In the Haber process the exothermic reaction N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ uses an iron catalyst, elevated pressure and a compromise temperature; cooling removes ammonia and unreacted gases are recycled. The Contact process oxidises SO₂ to SO₃ using vanadium(V) oxide, then absorbs SO₃ in sulfuric acid before controlled dilution. Know each raw material, transformation, separation and recycle stream rather than memorising one equation. Catalysts improve rate but do not shift equilibrium at fixed conditions. High pressure requires energy and stronger equipment, so its benefit must justify cost and risk. Industrial pollution controls can capture acidic gases, treat effluent and reduce waste. Use balanced equations to calculate theoretical yields, then account for incomplete conversion, recycling and losses separately. Never imply that a classroom apparatus model is a literal plant design.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

Why is a moderate temperature used in the Haber process rather than the lowest possible temperature?

Lower temperature favours the exothermic equilibrium yield but slows the reaction. A compromise temperature with a catalyst gives an economical production rate.

### Example 2

Why are unused nitrogen and hydrogen recycled after ammonia is separated?

Conversion in one pass is incomplete. Recycling gives unreacted feed further opportunities to react and reduces raw-material waste.

### Example 3

Explain why sulfur trioxide is not simply added directly to water in the Contact process.

Its highly exothermic reaction produces an acid mist that is hard to condense. It is absorbed in concentrated sulfuric acid to form oleum, then diluted carefully.

## Check your reasoning

Explain why the method applies before calculating or naming a result. Compare with a contrasting case. For calculations carry units, keep intermediate precision, then check by substitution, conservation or a second route. Describe observations separately from their explanation.
